extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (attorneys, agents) drafting or prosecuting patent claims, especially for computer-implemented inventions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting claim language, specifications, and drawings to avoid invocation of 35 U.S.C. § 112(f) (means-plus-function) and to ensure definiteness under § 112(b), with emphasis on computer-implemented inventions. Includes tests from Federal Circuit cases, examples of structural terms, and prosecution/claim-drafting tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Williamson standard — words understood as name for structure
rubrics_metrics.description: "The standard is whether the words of the claim are understood by persons of ordinary skill in the art to have a sufficiently definite meaning as the name for structure."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presumption that lack of the word "means" avoids §112(f) was weakened by Williamson; a claim term that does not use the word "means" can still invoke §112(f) if it fails to recite sufficiently definite structure. Evaluate whether POSITA would view the claim term as a structural name; if not, §112(f) may apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional language as candidates for §112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms that precede "configured to," "adapted to," or present participles ("-ing" words) may be candidates for functional interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting, stop to identify terms that may be considered functional. Such wording increases the risk the claim term will be treated as function-only and thus subject to §112(f). Consider recasting into structural language where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-level features must themselves connote structure
rubrics_metrics.description: If a term does not itself connote structure, determine whether the claim itself provides sufficient features to connote structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding structural detail into the claim (e.g., interactions between components, elements like "processor" + "memory" + modules) can in some cases avoid §112(f). Care: adding features can narrow claim scope and enable design-arounds; balance breadth vs structural detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification and figures must provide structural detail
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim and claim terms do not connote structure, determine whether the specification and figures provide a detailed definition and description such that POSITA concludes the term connotes structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe how components are connected, what data is passed, and what operations each component performs. Showing how components operate together (not merely listing functions) helps impart structural character to functional terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: If no structure identified, claim invokes §112(f) and must map to corresponding structure
rubrics_metrics.description: "If we are unable to identify any corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification, the claim term is indefinite."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once a term is treated as means-plus-function under §112(f), claim construction requires identification of the corresponding structure, material, or acts disclosed in the specification; failure to do so leads to indefiniteness under §112(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: For computer-implemented functions, disclose more than a general-purpose computer
rubrics_metrics.description: "Because these functions are computer-implemented functions, moreover, the structure disclosed in the specification must be more than a general purpose computer or microprocessor."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be definite, the specification must disclose an algorithm for performing the claimed computer-implemented function. Algorithms can be expressed as mathematical formulae, prose, flow charts, or other sufficiently specific forms. Mere statement that a general-purpose processor performs the function is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithm disclosure requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must disclose an algorithm for the claimed function; the algorithm may be expressed as mathematical formula, prose, flow chart, or any manner providing sufficient structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming functions performed by software or hardware, include concrete algorithms, flowcharts, pseudocode, or detailed procedural descriptions in the specification to identify corresponding structure and avoid indefiniteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of structural terms that courts have found not to invoke §112(f) (MPEP §2181(I)(A))
rubrics_metrics.description: MPEP lists examples of structural terms found not to invoke §112(f): "circuit," "detent mechanism," "digital detector," "reciprocating member," "connector assembly," "perforation," "sealingly connected joints," and "eyeglass hanger member."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent practitioners should consider using such terms where appropriate because they have been held to connote structure. Cite MPEP §2181(I)(A) and relevant cases (Mass. Inst. of Tech., Linear Tech., Apex, Greenberg, Personalized Media, CCS Fitness, Cole v. Kimberly‑Clark, Watts, Al‑Site) as persuasive authority for structural connotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer 'circuit' or 'circuitry' for computer-implemented inventions when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: For computer-implemented inventions, the term "circuit" or "circuitry" has consistently been found to connote structure and to avoid §112(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use "circuit"/"circuitry" coupled with description of the circuit's operation to convey structural arrangement of components; this typically conveys sufficient structure to avoid means-plus-function treatment. However, still provide detailed descriptions/algorithms where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution with 'processor'—may invoke §112(f) in some contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Many practitioners consider "processor" to connote structure, but the PTAB and courts have found instances where "processor" was interpreted to invoke §112(f), particularly if the claimed features cannot be performed by a general purpose processor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If features cannot be performed by a general‑purpose processor, invoking "processor" risks §112(f). PTAB cases (Ex Parte Lakkala, Ex Parte Erol, Ex Parte Smith, Ex Parte Cadarso) show the Office may raise new grounds of rejection based on §112(f) for claims using "processor." Consider reciting processor+memory+modules and describing modules in the spec (e.g., modules stored on memory and executable by processors) to reduce risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid describing modules only by the functions they perform
rubrics_metrics.description: Describing modules solely by the functions they perform (without structural detail) is insufficient to define the module as structural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit found the '033 patent indefinite because passages described functions of CPP modules but did not define 'compliance mechanism' in specific structural terms. Instead, describe how modules are implemented, how they interact, and structural interconnections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show how components 'operate' as a circuit/structural arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: In Inventio, what made 'modernizing device' structural was the specification's disclosure regarding how the device and its internal components operated as a circuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize operational descriptions (how internal components inter-operate) in the specification and drawings to impart structural significance to otherwise functional terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting trade-offs: add structural interaction vs claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: One way to save a claim from §112(f) interpretation may be to add more structure directly into the claim, where possible; but including superfluous features can adversely impact claim scope and invite design-arounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the benefit of adding structure against narrowing claim scope. Where possible, add interaction details that impart structure without unnecessarily limiting inventive scope (e.g., reciting relationships between processor and memory, or modules stored in memory and executable by processors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Five-step Federal Circuit analysis for functional claim language
rubrics_metrics.description: Court-provided steps: (1) identify term being claimed functionally, (2) determine whether the term is understood by one of ordinary skill in the art to connote structure, (3) if no, determine whether the claim itself provides sufficient features to connote structure, (4) if no, determine whether specification and figures provide detailed definition and description that POSITA concludes connotes structure, (5) if no, conclude that the claim invokes §112(f) and determine if the claim is definite under §112(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this analysis as a checklist when evaluating claim language during drafting or prosecution to decide whether the term will be treated as means-plus-function and whether the specification supports corresponding structure to avoid indefiniteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: If a term is treated as means-plus-function, identify corresponding structure/material/acts in the spec
rubrics_metrics.description: When a term is determined to be a means-plus-function element, attempt to construe the disputed claim term by identifying the corresponding material, acts, or structure described in the specification to which the claim term will be limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map each claimed function to specific passages, figures, algorithms, modules, or structural components in the spec. Absent such mapping, claims will be indefinite under §112(b).
